test.mechanism_chain: Reconstructed pay by source type does not show the proposed general pre-invention surge -> weakens the proposed general wage-surge premise. This does not identify the marginal labour-cost return to a particular machine or exclude wage incentives.
test.strongest_rival: Samples overrepresent institutional/part-time low-output labour, concealing a high-wage commercial cotton margin.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable full-time commercial cotton spinning records with counts and hours, versus institutional and other fibres.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S08 source definitions, records and regressions: no general surge, source-type gaps, sparse cotton observations; explicit limits preserved.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Wage levels, wage changes, daily earnings, hourly labour costs and returns to a particular machine are different measures. Sparse commercial cotton records and working-time assumptions leave the relevant marginal incentive unresolved; alternative invention motives in IND-S08 remain speculative.

statement: In 1835 Ure publicly advocated factory mechanisation partly as a means to substitute cheaper labour and reduce dependence on independent skilled workers.

sources.locator: extract paragraphs beginning “The principle of the factory system”, “By the infirmity”, and “In the infancy of mechanical engineering”; compiler original-page ranges 20–23, 29–31
sources.supports: Records contemporary managerial advocacy for skill substitution and tractability.

counterevidence: Skilled mechanics and machine operatives remained necessary; Ure is a partisan advocate whose welfare claims are not corroborated by this extract.
inference_limits: Shows a stated aspiration, not universal employer intention, successful complete deskilling or demonstrated worker benefit.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Kelly and Ó Gráda trace a pathway from instrument-making skill and precision measurement to complex textile machinery and the machine tools needed for repeated production and replacement parts.

sources.supports: Identifies skill transfer, gauges and exact tools, and the demand for reproducible wearing components.

counterevidence: The jenny and atmospheric engine could use less elaborate capabilities; cross-country tool histories have other routes and political contingencies.
inference_limits: A historically supported pathway rather than a universal prerequisite; no independent causal effect of national skill endowment is estimated.

test.mechanism_chain: Precision craft/measurement capabilities -> reproducible complicated components -> machinery supply and replacement -> sustained industrial use.
test.strongest_rival: Demand/capital expansion alone induces both tool skill and machinery; capabilities could be an outcome rather than prior constraint.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated personnel/tool transfers preceding new workable designs and matched sites with demand but missing skills.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S10 sections 2.1–2.3: named instrument/mechanic transfers, valve making and machine-tool/parts account; also simpler early artifacts acknowledged.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Demand and supply reinforce one another; broad national claims lack an exogenous comparison.

statement: Broadberry and Gupta’s reconstruction makes the timing of Lancashire’s competitive gains depend on raw-cotton and transport costs as well as wages and uneven productivity advances across spinning and weaving.

sources.supports: Reconstructs comparative wages, productivity proxies, raw cotton prices and market-specific delivery costs.

counterevidence: Indian productivity stagnation is assumed for key intervals, and household earnings and labour units are not directly comparable; political market access remains a rival/complement.
inference_limits: Applies to the inspected 2005 model and reconstruction, not directly measured productivity for all Indian textiles or proof of tariffs’ irrelevance.

test.mechanism_chain: Productivity rises unevenly and cotton/freight costs change -> relative delivered cost shifts -> merchants source differently -> competitive reversal.
test.strongest_rival: Colonial policy and coercive market access could drive the same trade shifts without equivalent cost advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Quality-matched delivered costs and shares across markets with different policy but similar transport, before and after price changes.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S11 pp. 16–25 and conclusion; compared IND-S13 policy testimony. The cost model includes cotton/freight but assumes some Indian productivity paths.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Policy shapes prices and markets; quality and labour-unit comparability remain incomplete.

statement: Clingingsmith and Williamson propose that pre-1810 Indian textile decline involved domestic political/agricultural shocks, while later decline involved stronger international manufactured-price pressure.

sources.supports: Uses a three-sector model and relative-price evidence to propose two phases.

counterevidence: Regional political histories and data are uneven; colonial intervention, quality changes and capital constraints are not independently isolated by these prices.
inference_limits: Model assumptions include mobile labour, subsistence-linked pay and initially non-traded grain. This is an interpretation, not exogenous identification of drought or Mughal decline.

test.mechanism_chain: Domestic agricultural/political shock -> dear grain and subsistence-linked nominal wages -> reduced textile competitiveness; later world textile prices add pressure.
test.strongest_rival: Colonial interventions or textile demand shifts could alter prices and employment without the posited agricultural cause.
test.discriminating_observation: District timing: independently measured harvest/drought/conflict shocks preceding wage pressure and textile contraction, including low-shock controls.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S12 model and relative-price/timing argument; no independently identified district treatment comparison found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Modelled labour mobility and wage linkage do causal work; price data alone fit multiple mechanisms.

statement: Inikori argues that Atlantic demand linked to slavery-based commodity production helped form the markets and regional expansion within which British cotton mechanisation developed.

sources.locator: sections I–III, especially section II paragraphs on Lancashire’s wages and Atlantic export sales
sources.supports: Connects regional protoindustry, Atlantic demand and later mechanisation.

counterevidence: Factor prices, domestic demand, engineering and other trading regions also matter; regional wage rankings do not by themselves adjudicate international wage comparisons.
inference_limits: An attributed historical mechanism, not a quantified necessary contribution of slavery to each invention. Export demand is not the same variable as investment finance.

test.mechanism_chain: Slavery-linked Atlantic commodity trade -> expanding markets -> regional protoindustry growth -> investment and mechanisation incentives.
test.strongest_rival: Domestic markets, factor prices or engineering can explain innovation; Atlantic demand might follow rather than precede industrial advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Regional/sectoral demand exposure preceding investment, with comparable low-exposure producers and separate supply/finance channels.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S13 regional wage/exports sequence and IND-S11 competition account; temporal market linkage found, no isolated necessity test.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Atlantic markets, shipping, wages and political power are reciprocally connected; export shares are not investment causality.

statement: Inikori’s discussion of Charles Grant’s 1821 testimony identifies asymmetric British and Indian tariff power as a contemporary concern alongside improvements in machinery.

sources.locator: section IV, Charles Grant paragraph immediately preceding table 3
sources.supports: Reproduces an explicit contemporary argument about protection at home and political power over Indian imports.

counterevidence: The testimony does not establish a tariff counterfactual for each cloth quality or exclude cost-driven competitive shifts.
inference_limits: Primary testimony is accessed through Inikori’s quotation via Chaudhuri; original parliamentary record not independently inspected. No causal magnitude assigned.

test.mechanism_chain: Imperial tariff authority -> asymmetric protection/import permission -> altered producer choice set and market access.
test.strongest_rival: Productivity and freight advantages alone would produce the same import shift under symmetric sovereignty.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable products under differing tariff regimes and original legislative/merchant records on excluded choices.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Grant testimony as reproduced in IND-S13 section IV; sought original-record specificity but did not acquire parliamentary source.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Testimony establishes awareness and constrained sovereignty more firmly than the counterfactual trade magnitude.

statement: Japanese mills in the 1890s adapted ring spinning through a package involving cotton imports, mixed fibres, more preparation labour and a changed labour force, rather than merely copying American operating conditions.

sources.supports: Combines order specifications with historical accounts of cotton preparation and workforce change.

counterevidence: Cotton prices, yarn markets and suppliers changed concurrently; order specifications are not direct measurements of realised mill productivity.
inference_limits: Does not establish the separate effect of each component, or that the labour arrangements were freely chosen or beneficial to workers.

test.mechanism_chain: Imported fibre variety plus labour-intensive mixing -> reduced breakage/broader fibre control -> viable rings under Japanese conditions.
test.strongest_rival: Changes in machine design or yarn demand alone could improve performance without preparation reorganisation.
test.discriminating_observation: Within comparable machinery and yarn counts, mixing adoption precedes improved throughput/breakage; costs and work hours measured.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S14 pp. 549–551, order table and contemporary observations: timing of mixed-cotton orders and package change support the pathway.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Order proxies do not independently identify labour, fibres and design; exact realised productivity not observed.

statement: Between 1878 and 1914 mule and ring spinning both continued to improve; Saxonhouse and Wright interpret British mule persistence as a choice supported by skills and product flexibility, not simply stagnant technology.

sources.supports: Documents coexisting technologies, skill requirements and adoption models using changing technical frontiers.

counterevidence: Rings later gained capabilities and mule performance growth slowed; rationality at one time does not demonstrate optimal long-run investment.
inference_limits: Technical specification proxies and nonexperimental firm-choice models do not isolate learning, and the authors’ strong claim about unavoidable British decline is not adopted here.

test.mechanism_chain: Mule-specific skills and continuing machine improvement -> sustained capability -> continued purchases where advantageous.
test.strongest_rival: Entrenched employers/unions or sunk capital produce persistence despite inferior returns.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare realised quality-adjusted profits and best-practice improvements in new mule purchases versus feasible rings, not only old stocks.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S14 performance specifications and choice model: both technologies improve before 1914 and multiple countries buy mules.
test.remaining_ambiguity: New orders weaken a pure obsolete-stock story but may still reflect expectations, omitted costs or institutional constraints.

statement: India supplied the largest number of high-draft machinery orders in Saxonhouse and Wright’s 1929–1933 dataset, a bounded counterexample to equating low wages with non-adoption of labour-saving equipment.

sources.supports: Reports destination ordering and qualifications to the labour-relations explanation.

counterevidence: Order count is not an installed-stock share or necessarily a comparable fraction of each country’s capacity.
inference_limits: Restricted to the supplier dataset and interval; the paper’s proposed male-workforce/labour-relations mechanism remains tentative.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: In late Qing and Republican China, some handweavers combined machine-spun warp with hand-spun weft, and cheaper factory yarn also supported handloom weaving in new districts.

sources.supports: Describes mixed yarn use, Dingxian and geographical expansion of hand weaving.

counterevidence: Hand spinning declined and factory cloth increased its share; hybrid persistence differed by region and product.
inference_limits: Earlier studies underlying Eyferth’s historical background were not independently acquired; no nationwide adoption rate is inferred from the examples.

test.mechanism_chain: Cheap machine yarn -> replace selected spinning inputs -> handloom production retains product functions and expands accessible supply.
test.strongest_rival: General market growth alone may sustain hand weaving; poor households may simply be unable to buy cloth.
test.discriminating_observation: Yarn-price/access changes preceding weaving expansion, with product-level evidence of mixed warp/weft and comparison to inaccessible districts.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S15 pp. 373–374: explicit mixed yarn and named new weaving districts; original local studies not independently acquired.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Price, population, cash and fabric differences interact; mechanism stronger than national quantitative effect.

statement: Eyferth reports that handloom cloth accounted for about 70 percent of China’s cotton textile output in 1934–1936, despite the expansion of factory production.

sources.supports: Provides the bounded period and output denominator for the reported estimate.

counterevidence: Handloom market share was declining and aggregation may mask regional variation; the underlying estimation method was not audited.
inference_limits: An attributed estimate from earlier research, not a newly verified census; cannot equate output share with employment share or household welfare.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Eyferth documents moral and gendered classifications of textile work in late imperial and Republican China, including reform rhetoric that rendered household female production economically invisible.

sources.supports: Contrasts gendered household ideals, diverse practice and later reformist definitions of productive work.

counterevidence: Actual household divisions were more varied than prescriptive discourse; beliefs alone need not explain persistence when cash, prices and employment differ.
inference_limits: Documents classifications and interpretation, not freely expressed worker preferences. Post-1949 rationing mechanisms are excluded from this pre-1950 case.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: American factory electrification included distinct line-shaft, group-drive and unit-drive arrangements; replacing a prime mover with a motor did not automatically reorganise factory power distribution.

sources.supports: Documents the configurations, early retrofits and the functional differences.

counterevidence: Group drive remained useful in some applications, and older configurations survived beyond the main transition.
inference_limits: The engineering distinction is well documented; it supplies neither an exact date for universal replacement nor proof that all firms benefited from unit drive.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Devine links effective unit-drive use to compatible machinery, production redesign, utility expansion and application services, with sunk onsite equipment differentiating retrofits from new plants.

sources.locator: pp. 363, 368–371; machine redesign and Detroit Edison paragraphs
sources.supports: Describes indirect production benefits, compatibility constraints and services offered with electricity.

counterevidence: Firms varied in load, process and existing capital; some group-drive choices remained justified. Expanding firms may have selected electrification.
inference_limits: Not causal identification of all postwar productivity gains; worker pace, discretion and welfare are not assessed by the engineering evidence.

test.mechanism_chain: Compatible motors/tools plus redesign and service -> flexible local power -> productive reorganisation -> adoption benefits.
test.strongest_rival: Demand-led expansion or new capital generally causes both redesign and productivity, with motors only accompanying it.
test.discriminating_observation: Matched retrofits/new plants measuring workflow and output before/after, with comparable non-electric new equipment.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S16 configuration history, redesign comments and utility installation services; evidence for needed complements found, no clean experiment.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Selective engineering cases and firm growth can bias productivity interpretation; unit drive not always superior.

statement: Devine reports that electric motors represented roughly one-quarter of US manufacturing mechanical-drive horsepower in 1909 and over half in 1919; he separately infers unit-drive diffusion because comprehensive configuration statistics were unavailable.

sources.supports: Provides the capacity denominator and explains indirect evidence for unit-drive timing.

counterevidence: Installed capacity is not utilisation, output, establishment adoption or the source of electricity generation.
inference_limits: Reuses the bounded historical series, not a reconstructed census; motor adoption must not be counted as complete factory redesign.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: The AT&T historical study attributes delayed switching automation to organisational interdependencies and market-scale economics, rather than treating invention as immediate deployability.

sources.supports: States adaptation and larger-market profitability mechanisms.

counterevidence: Technology improvement and market growth were intertwined.
inference_limits: Abstract-level support; relative causal weights not audited.

test.mechanism_chain: Interdependent manual service -> firm/technology adaptation -> viable switching at suitable scale -> staged adoption
test.strongest_rival: Purely technical improvement or wage-cost changes could drive timing without independent organisational causation.
test.discriminating_observation: Internal plans and comparable exchanges with different organisational readiness or market size.
test.evidence_sought_found: LBR-S01 abstract reports archival interpretation; full mechanism evidence was not acquired, so no adjudication claimed.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The contribution cannot rank organisational adaptation versus technical and economic change.

statement: In the telephone-automation study, incumbent operators and later young female cohorts experienced different labour-market outcomes; stable later-cohort employment did not mean incumbent workers were unharmed.

sources.supports: Linked incumbent outcomes differ from repeated-cohort employment findings.

counterevidence: Genealogical linkage is non-random; the authors report robustness and weighting rather than eliminating every possible selection process.
inference_limits: Inference is conditional on comparison/selection assumptions; not a universal automation result.

test.mechanism_chain: Dial cutover removes switching jobs -> incumbents lose specialised job opportunity -> adverse decade-later employment/occupational outcomes, while future entrants reallocate
test.strongest_rival: Different local demand trends or non-random linkage/selection could explain cutover timing and measured incumbent outcomes. Such trends should also appear in comparable local controls or pre-cutover outcomes; selection should be sensitive to linkage and weighting checks.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare linked incumbents with local matched controls separately from future cohorts around cutover timing; inspect pre-trends, alternative controls and linkage/weighting robustness. These checks constrain but do not eliminate unobserved selection.
test.evidence_sought_found: LBR-S02 §§III,VI,VII inspected; study uses these distinct designs and reports different outcomes.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Unobserved local changes, linked-sample selection and incomplete wages remain possible limitations.

statement: The main later-cohort comparison focuses on white American-born women aged 16–25, while incumbent operators are followed through a separate linked census sample; neither sample directly represents all affected workers.

sources.supports: Defines populations and separate linkage strategy.

counterevidence: The paper includes additional robustness populations, but the main population remains bounded.
inference_limits: Do not generalise to all women, racial groups, immigrants or displaced workers.

test.reason: Reports a bounded measurement/design or author argument; no new causal effect asserted.

statement: The authors find no clear overall wage effect for later young female cohorts, but the relevant tests cannot exclude wage changes around plus or minus 10 percent; no detected effect is not proof of unchanged pay.

sources.supports: Explicitly discusses power and wide bounds in smaller wage-analysis sample.

counterevidence: Heterogeneous effects and measurement noise could mask changes.
inference_limits: Applies to these wage tests, not an exact confidence interval for every subgroup.

test.reason: Reports a bounded measurement/design or author argument; no new causal effect asserted.

statement: The roughly 60 percent estimate of 2018 US employment in job titles added since 1940 is an imputation from new-title shares within occupations, not a direct count of workers in new micro-titles.

sources.supports: Explains the estimate and unavailable micro-title employment counts.

counterevidence: Index revisions and within-occupation title weighting affect measurement.
inference_limits: Do not restate as 60 percent of occupations invented since 1940, or as identified jobs caused by technology.

test.reason: Reports a bounded measurement/design or author argument; no new causal effect asserted.

statement: The new-work study links title emergence to both output-complementing innovation and demand shifts; its patent-based categories may overlap and cannot exhaust technological change.

sources.supports: Defines exposure limitations and estimates augmentation/demand relationships.

counterevidence: Automation and augmentation exposures are positively correlated; classification itself may contribute to overlap.
inference_limits: A US constructed-data study; neither title novelty nor patent similarity alone proves an accessible job opportunity.

test.mechanism_chain: Changed productive possibilities or market demand -> changed tasks/output -> new job specialties and employment allocation
test.strongest_rival: Relabelling and classification changes, or shared demand trends, could create apparent new work without substantive new tasks.
test.discriminating_observation: Check source-title consistency and compare innovation/demand exposures with placebo timing and alternative specifications.
test.evidence_sought_found: LBR-S03 §II and Tables IV/V discuss construction, IV and placebo strategies; raw data not replicated.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Classification and identification assumptions remain; title addition does not directly measure worker entry costs or bargaining.

statement: A task-allocation model distinguishes labour displacement, productivity effects and creation of new labour tasks; positive productivity alone need not imply increased labour demand.

sources.supports: Sets out the model channels and their distinct implications.

counterevidence: Aggregate demand, ownership, institutions and adjustment alter realised outcomes.
inference_limits: This is a model distinction, not an unconditional causal claim about every technology.

test.reason: Reports a bounded measurement/design or author argument; no new causal effect asserted.

statement: Xianrendong pottery-bearing contexts were dated to approximately 20,000–19,000 calibrated years BP, long before farming; this dates surviving use, not the invention of pottery.

sources.supports: Associated bone/charcoal dates and micromorphological checks of the deposits.

counterevidence: The dated materials are associated deposits; some strata were affected by small-scale bioturbation.
inference_limits: No first inventor, unique origin, or regional prevalence follows from this site.

test.reason: Reports contextual dating, not a causal explanation of adoption.

statement: Xianrendong fragments document vessel-making among foragers, while exterior burning makes cooking plausible rather than identifying particular foods.

sources.supports: Forager context, temper, forming methods, and burned exterior surfaces.

counterevidence: No reconstructed complete vessels or direct residue identification in this study.
inference_limits: Multiple sherds do not establish routine household deployment or mass production.

test.reason: Describes vessel evidence and a qualified use inference, not why people adopted pottery.

statement: The Japanese sample maintained a strong aquatic-processing association across the Pleistocene–Holocene transition, challenging a simple account in which pottery expanded principally to process newly abundant terrestrial foods.

sources.supports: 801 samples across 46 sites; conservative aquatic assignments of 73/156 and 256/566 lipid-bearing samples in the two periods.

counterevidence: Plant foods and low-lipid contents are imperfectly detectable; functional continuity need not imply unchanged diet.
inference_limits: The sample concerns surviving sampled ceramics, not shares of all food or all households; motives remain interpretive.

test.mechanism_chain: Warming changes available foods -> users adopt/use more pots for new terrestrial processing -> pottery expands and contents diversify. The evidence tests the predicted functional change.
test.strongest_rival: Continued aquatic processing with changing fishing practices or social conventions also permits ceramic expansion.
test.discriminating_observation: Time-matched, preservation-controlled changes in plant/terrestrial versus aquatic residues, combined with independent food availability and vessel production measures.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S02 explicitly tested environmental/period expectations and found strong aquatic continuity; it did not identify every pot’s contents or measure all household use.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Poorly detected plants and lipid mixing remain possible; residue continuity cannot by itself identify a psychological cultural norm.

statement: In the surveyed southern Levant contexts, utilitarian iron appears in Iron I but becomes dominant among classified metal tools/weapons only in Iron IIA, while bronze manufacture continues.

sources.locator: pp. 286–294; abstract; Iron Production during the Iron IIA
sources.supports: Contextual counts distinguish initial use from tenth–ninth-century BCE dominance and continuing bronze work.

counterevidence: Recovery, corrosion and recycling differ by metal and context.
inference_limits: Archaeological assemblage dominance is not a regional household adoption percentage.

test.reason: Reports chronology and assemblage composition rather than a cause.

statement: The southern Levant evidence weakens an explanation that a general bronze-input shortage forced the transition: copper production continued and the authors report persistent tin-bronze compositions.

sources.supports: Arabah copper chronology and 95 copper-alloy objects with reported average tin contents maintained around 5–6 wt%.

counterevidence: The 95-object chemical dataset was unpublished; scarcity could affect prices or places without changing surviving alloy percentages.
inference_limits: Does not disprove every local or short-lived supply disruption; neither prices nor access distributions are observed.

test.mechanism_chain: Bronze inputs become generally scarce -> producers/users substitute iron -> iron gains use. The claim tests the broad scarcity premise.
test.strongest_rival: Continued bronze supply plus changed iron production organisation can yield the same transition without general shortage.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated procurement interruptions or price/access deterioration preceding substitution, contrasted with areas retaining supply.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S03 pp. 298–299 reports copper-production continuity and maintained alloy tin levels; prices and distribution were not found, and the tin dataset is unpublished there.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Stable composition can coexist with scarcity, higher prices or selective allocation; geographically local shocks remain possible.

statement: The inspected Canaan study does not find a heat-treatment breakthrough that accounts for iron dominance; carbon content alone is insufficient evidence of deliberate superior steelmaking.

sources.supports: Metallography, corrosion limits, spontaneous carburisation, and absence of a clear chronological technical leap.

counterevidence: Preservation restricts metallography; exceptional objects may escape the sample.
inference_limits: Failure to detect a breakthrough does not prove equal cost, durability, repairability or battlefield performance.

test.mechanism_chain: Improved heat treatment -> reliably superior iron objects -> users replace bronze. The claim tests a chronological breakthrough.
test.strongest_rival: More reliable/available iron supply or institutional demand can expand use without a new heat-treatment threshold.
test.discriminating_observation: A well-dated step change in treatment and task-specific performance preceding adoption, with comparable preservation and alloy alternatives.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S03 pp. 295–300 reports no clear technical leap in sampled material and explains carbon/corrosion ambiguities.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Corrosion, unpublished detail and missing exceptional workshops may hide changes; hardness alone is not complete performance.

statement: Iron work associated with older bronze-working areas and public architecture makes local craft adaptation and administrative support plausible contributors to systematic production.

sources.supports: Spatial/chronological association of metalworking and evidence for urban smelting or forging.

counterevidence: Iron I production remains are lacking; imported iron or mobile specialists remain possible.
inference_limits: Workshop location alone neither identifies ownership nor demonstrates compulsion, funding or a state monopoly.

test.mechanism_chain: Existing metal skills plus administrative support -> local smelting/forging capacity -> sustained iron production and wider use.
test.strongest_rival: Co-location may reflect ordinary urban facilities or market access, while iron demand draws administrations to existing work.
test.discriminating_observation: Sequenced production investment, inventories, institutional orders or controlled access preceding expansion; comparison with independent workshops.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S03 documents metalworking continuity and public-architecture association, but no contracts or direct ownership evidence.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Reverse causation and shared urban location fit the record; early production remains are sparse.

statement: Chinese iron history requires separate chronologies for meteoritic objects, bloomery production, casting and practical cast-iron implements; later finds revised earlier accounts of a wholly southern, cast-iron beginning.

sources.supports: Explicit revision of the author’s previous reconstruction.
Differentiates first appearance, production and functional use, with disputed dates.

counterevidence: Early object dating and production identification remain contested; surviving objects do not locate first smelters.
inference_limits: Supports branching stages, not a definite single transmission route or inventor.

test.reason: Describes distinctions in evidence and changes in scholarship; no transmission mechanism asserted.

statement: Chinese cast-iron production plausibly combined iron smelting with bronze-casting and ceramic/kiln expertise, but the claim that political suppression explains the absence of alternative iron routes remains a hypothesis.

sources.locator: sections on cast-iron annealing and Access to technology; concluding discussion
sources.supports: Proposes cross-craft integration and discusses moulds, kilns, fuel, labour and state power.
Earlier hypothesis connecting agricultural implement forms with iron casting.

counterevidence: The 2025 comparison aggregates diverse regions and infers institutions partly from outcomes.
inference_limits: No comparative cost accounts or direct policy enforcement evidence here identify the causal contribution of suppression.

test.mechanism_chain: Links among smelting, casting and ceramic expertise -> controlled casting/treatment -> practical cast-iron output; state support may organise this bundle.
test.strongest_rival: Local ore/task economics and independent craft exchange could create the same bundle without coercive political suppression.
test.discriminating_observation: Securely phased co-located processes and independent evidence of organisation; competing production under/away from claimed restrictions.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S15 proposes the bundle and stronger political account; MAT-S04 documents revised early histories. No enforcement archive was inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Facilities identify technical contributions more securely than ownership, suppression or counterfactual western failure.

statement: Song–Yuan mineral fuel in iron manufacture is supported by texts and anomalously old carbon dates in castings, but a universal shift to coke, or one exact production route, is not established.

sources.supports: Su Shi text, sulphur evidence, radiocarbon results, and distinction between smelting and remelting.

counterevidence: Charcoal remained possible in other furnaces; carbon can enter during remelting as well as smelting.
inference_limits: Neither national adoption share nor coal/coke ratio follows from the few dated objects.

test.reason: Describes support for mineral-fuel use and its observational limits.

statement: The often-repeated large estimate of Song iron output is not a secure observation: Wagner explicitly rejects the reliability of the extrapolation from state quota figures.

sources.supports: Discusses the roughly 115,000 metric tonne estimate and its flawed underlying assumptions.

counterevidence: The author considers the magnitude plausible; criticism does not establish low output.
inference_limits: Do not use disputed output as a denominator for productivity or an adoption rate.

test.reason: Reports an explicit methodological criticism of an estimate.

statement: Meroe replica smelts improved after changes in ore, air delivery and operation, demonstrating coupled operating constraints rather than the sufficiency of a copied furnace shape.

sources.supports: Failed/low-yield trials, changes to ores and bellows, viable later operation and explicit experimental limitations.

counterevidence: Parameters changed together; some later successes lacked detailed records.
inference_limits: Modern reconstructed feasibility does not identify the unique ancient process or provide an ancient output series.

test.mechanism_chain: Suitable ore plus adjusted blast/charging and operator coordination -> better reduction/slag behaviour -> more workable products in replica trials.
test.strongest_rival: Different modern operating choices could also succeed; apparent improvement could result from one unisolated variable rather than the whole historical reconstruction.
test.discriminating_observation: Controlled replication changing one parameter at a time, matching archaeological residues and retaining detailed mass balances.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S06 Tables 2–4 and Lessons Learned record failed/low-yield runs and improved combinations; authors flag anecdotal later data.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Joint changes prevent attribution to each input; viability is demonstrated only for tested modern configurations, not a unique ancient procedure.

statement: Charcoal analysis at Meroe and Hamadab shows persistent, selective use of Acacia type nilotica in metallurgical contexts across a long production history.

sources.supports: 1,754 analysed charcoal fragments overall; strong metallurgical dominance contrasted with limited non-metallurgical assemblages.

counterevidence: Comparison contexts are small and not always contemporaneous; taxonomic identification sometimes tentative.
inference_limits: Persistent fuel selection does not by itself prove woodland management, local sourcing or unchanged production intensity.

test.reason: Describes observed charcoal selection over dated contexts.

statement: Meroe’s charcoal assemblages do not establish smelting-induced deforestation; stable fuel access is compatible with management, lower intensity, efficient operation or imports.

sources.supports: Authors explicitly enumerate alternative supply explanations and unknown exchange range.

counterevidence: Ecological degradation could coexist with continued access through a widening collection catchment.
inference_limits: No landscape-scale vegetation reconstruction or procurement-cost series is supplied; absence of a charcoal signal is not proof of ecological harmlessness.

test.mechanism_chain: Sustained iron demand -> heavy local wood removal -> depletion/changed fuel use or production decline; charcoal should register some consequences if local sourcing persists.
test.strongest_rival: Managed regeneration, smaller output, efficient operation or fuel imports maintain selected charcoal despite different local ecological conditions.
test.discriminating_observation: Independent vegetation history and charcoal provenance/procurement radius alongside dated production intensity.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S07 finds persistent selection and explicitly enumerates alternative supply explanations, with no demonstrated shortage signal.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Imports or expanding catchments can hide local degradation; charcoal selectivity is not a woodland census.

statement: Controlled comparisons show that tin bronze’s greater possible hardness does not make it universally superior to arsenical bronze; ductility and sheet-forming performance can favour the latter.

sources.supports: Mechanical tests and comparison with thin-sheet fabrication traditions.

counterevidence: Some tests need more reproducible elongation measurements; alloy concentration and processing strongly affect results.
inference_limits: Modern mechanical advantage is not a complete explanation of archaeological selection or user value.

test.mechanism_chain: Alloy composition and working treatment -> different hardness/ductility/toughness -> different suitability for specified sheet-forming tasks.
test.strongest_rival: A universal tin-bronze superiority account predicts better performance across relevant tasks, rather than a trade-off.
test.discriminating_observation: Controlled processing of both alloys followed by relevant mechanical tests and task failure assessment.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S08 directly tests alloys and identifies different advantages; pp. 500–508 discuss limits of elongation data.
test.remaining_ambiguity: This tests material behaviour, not whether historical smiths selected it for the inferred reason or whether costs favoured it.

statement: Experimental cosmelting of Peruvian copper oxides with arsenic-bearing sulphide ores produced usable copper–arsenic alloys across multiple mixtures, supplying a feasible alternative to a separate roasting sequence.

sources.supports: Crucible/furnace tests without pre-roasting or added flux and discussion of naturally mixed versus deliberately mixed ores.

counterevidence: Feasible experiments do not show which ancient workshops used this process or how often.
inference_limits: No universal origin sequence, automatic intention, ancient occupational-exposure level or cost advantage can be inferred.

test.reason: Describes achieved modern experimental feasibility, not a causal historical adoption account.

statement: The Andean history summarized by Lechtman includes continued arsenical-bronze use alongside Inka tin bronze, making coexistence and political distribution more appropriate than a complete superior-alloy replacement story.

sources.supports: Regional ore geography, coexistence and interpretation of Inka alloy distribution.

counterevidence: Underlying mine-control and closure evidence was not independently audited in this contribution.
inference_limits: Political explanation is plausible but not identified against transport costs, ore supply and task-specific demand.

test.mechanism_chain: Imperial access/control over tin and distribution -> supply of tin bronze across political space -> partial substitution with local continuities.
test.strongest_rival: Ore geography, transport costs and task performance can generate regional compositions without imperial standardisation as the primary cause.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable sites before/after incorporation, official versus local products, and independently established control of mines/flows.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S08 pp. 477–479 reports coexistence and interprets political distribution; underlying local-control studies not independently inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Political and resource effects likely interact; no identified causal effect or complete displacement.

statement: Hosler’s West Mexican studies describe tools as well as objects whose sound and colour mattered, so technological performance cannot be reduced to cutting hardness or military lethality.

sources.supports: Distinguishes tools/status items and relates bells and metallic colours to ritual and war symbolism.
Mechanical/physical properties and American object selection.

counterevidence: The 1995 full text was not acquired; frequency and direct historical passages have not been audited.
inference_limits: Does not establish that every object was ritual, that all consumers shared values, or that productive utility was absent.

test.mechanism_chain: Particular sonic/visual values -> patrons/users select bells and colours -> smiths develop relevant material properties.
test.strongest_rival: Functional availability, general display demand or analyst selection may produce similar assemblages without shared specific beliefs.
test.discriminating_observation: Object-level material choices combined with independently contextualised historical/linguistic evidence and non-elite comparisons.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S10 abstract states laboratory and ethnohistoric interpretation; MAT-S08 discusses American physical properties. Full symbolic argument unavailable.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No independently audited belief evidence here; not every consumer or object need share the proposed meanings.

statement: Hosler proposed South/Central American transmission into West Mexico combined with local technical transformation; this is a claim about selective recombination, not passive copying.

sources.supports: Two proposed phases of technical links and explicit local reinterpretation.

counterevidence: Only abstract read; dates differ between the 1988 and 1995 formulations. Similarity alone cannot exclude convergence.
inference_limits: Transfer route and carriers remain unverified here; neither isolation nor a complete imported package is assumed.

test.mechanism_chain: Interregional contact -> movement of know-how/components -> local recombination -> distinctive West Mexican production.
test.strongest_rival: Convergence from similar resources/tasks can create similarities without the proposed transfer; object movement alone may not transmit skills.
test.discriminating_observation: Diagnostic production sequences, intermediate chronology, source/provenance and contact evidence evaluated together.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S11 abstract proposes two transmission phases and transformations; detailed supporting catalogue unavailable.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Neither routes, carriers nor first dates independently verified; similarity alone fits several accounts.

statement: Chemical study of 52 Igbo Olokun beads supports locally distinctive glass groups; related beads elsewhere support exchange, while imported glass at other Ile-Ife sites rules out a wholly isolated setting.

sources.supports: Selected-sample chemistry, local raw-material compatibility, regional distribution and other-site soda-lime glass.

counterevidence: 52 beads are a small selected fraction; deposits disturbed; compatible raw materials are not a uniquely sourced quarry.
inference_limits: No import share for the entire city, market size, annual output or proven transmission of production skills follows.

test.mechanism_chain: Local glass production -> beads circulate through exchange -> related chemical groups occur elsewhere.
test.strongest_rival: Multiple makers using similar raw materials or redistribution from an unlocated production centre could share chemical signatures.
test.discriminating_observation: Distinctive trace patterns tied to production debris and secure regional chronology; tests of other potential sources.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S13 reports local bead chemistry, production debris and regional matches, with imported glass in other city contexts.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Local production is well supported, but origin of every distant bead and direction/organisation of exchange are not uniquely identified.

statement: Ile-Ife glass crucibles were specialised ceramic complements; reported usable capacities are evidence of batch capability, not a measurement of sustained industrial throughput.

sources.supports: Ten analysed samples, refractory clay, estimated 1–7 L usable capacities.

counterevidence: Body tables not acquired; vessel reconstruction and actual fill levels carry uncertainty.
inference_limits: Do not multiply capacity by an invented number of firings, workshops or years.

test.reason: Describes reported crucible capacities and measurement scope.

statement: Incompletely reacted glass batch on Ile-Ife crucibles directly strengthens the case for local primary glassmaking, while recipe uniqueness alone cannot establish an origin independent of all external ideas.

sources.locator: accepted manuscript pp. 2–4, Laboratory analysis and Implications
sources.supports: Residual quartz/feldspar, new reaction phases and heterogeneous glass distinguish raw-batch melting from only remelting finished imports.
Locally compatible recipe and participation in exchange.

counterevidence: Museum-store fragments lack newly excavated sealed contexts; authors advance a stronger autonomous-origin interpretation.
inference_limits: Local primary production is better established than the exact invention date, transmission history or subsequent disappearance.

test.reason: Identifies material evidence of a production operation; does not claim an adoption cause or independent-invention mechanism.

statement: Recycling and composite manufacture complicate inferences from surviving iron objects to initial production, replacement rates or material scarcity.

sources.locator: Introduction; Iron production and the forms of iron recycling; Conclusions
sources.supports: Detection problems and selected examples of reused iron; distinction between manufacture and reuse.

counterevidence: Some structural evidence is consistent with new composite manufacture as well as recycling.
inference_limits: A methodological warning, not a recycling percentage for either case; selective later parallels are not proof of earlier local practice.

test.mechanism_chain: Reuse/composite fabrication -> multiple material histories within surviving objects -> object count/chemistry does not uniquely identify new production.
test.strongest_rival: New composite manufacture without old scrap can produce some similar structures; differential preservation also changes counts.
test.discriminating_observation: Diagnostic reused fragments or incompatible material histories, compared with production structures of known new composites.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S16 supplies selected examples and explicitly warns that common manufacturing features can mimic recycling.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Methodological non-identifiability is supported; no recycling rate or actual local pathway is measured for MAT-C02/C03.

statement: Across these purposively selected cases, repeatable processes, complementary crafts and task-specific demand are better-supported comparison variables than a universal ranking of materials.

sources.supports: Functional persistence despite changes in availability.
Coupled operating variables.
Task-dependent alloy properties.
Local raw-material transformation.

counterevidence: Selection emphasises contrasting outcomes and cannot estimate how frequently any mechanism dominated.
inference_limits: A research framework rather than causal identification, universal law or forecast.

test.mechanism_chain: Task requirements and accessible complementary operations -> workable production/adoption choices -> branching and coexisting technologies.
test.strongest_rival: Different episodes may instead be dominated by independent resource shocks or political power; purposive selection may overstate recurrence.
test.discriminating_observation: Matched task/region contrasts with failed production, available alternatives and independent measures of demand/institutions.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S02, S06, S08 and S14 supply different kinds of bounded evidence; they do not constitute a representative comparative design.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cross-case recurrence is not causal identification; outcomes and source survival affect selection.

statement: Early eighteenth-century reports connect British variolation discussions to Ottoman practitioners, including women, and African expertise conveyed through Onesimus; this is evidence of transmission rather than a British origin.

sources.locator: Inoculation in parts of the Ottoman Empire and Europe
sources.supports: Reproduces the relevant reports and correspondence.

counterevidence: Surviving elite intermediaries may obscure earlier local transmission.
inference_limits: No continental prevalence, precise birthplace or unique transmission route is inferred.

test.reason: Bounded statement about documented knowledge channels, not their causal share in uptake.

statement: The inspected variolation evidence does not establish a unique origin or secure ancient chronology.

sources.locator: Inoculation in China and India; Conclusions
sources.supports: Contradictory testimony, different methods and uncertain early dates.

counterevidence: Boylston proposes a common route, but labels parts speculative.
inference_limits: Neither silence in surviving texts nor similarity of methods proves absence or common descent.

test.mechanism_chain: Sparse surviving accounts -> reconstruction of routes -> uncertain origin attribution
test.strongest_rival: Independent development or earlier undocumented diffusion also fits surviving accounts
test.discriminating_observation: Contemporaneous dated descriptions with identifiable technique and transmission contacts
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S01 checked early-origin claims against its source criticism; found uncertainty and conjecture
test.remaining_ambiguity: Original local-language records not independently inspected.

statement: Ottoman vaccination policy combined free provision commitments, multilingual instruction and religious endorsement before and alongside later compulsory rules.

sources.supports: 1840 free-provision decree, 1845 endorsement and 1846 multilingual treatise.

counterevidence: Policy texts describe intended provision, not universal performance.
inference_limits: No effect size for price, education or religious messaging is identified.

test.reason: Describes documented policy instruments, not their effectiveness.

statement: Ottoman universal-vaccination ambitions were constrained by vaccine production, personnel and rural delivery capacity; legal scope exceeded documented implementation.

sources.supports: Contrasts legislative expansion with production and staffing limitations.

counterevidence: Fear and refusal, instability and war could also depress uptake.
inference_limits: No district panel separates supply, trust and coercion effects.

test.mechanism_chain: Wide mandate plus limited supplies/staff -> inability to deliver repeatedly -> incomplete coverage
test.strongest_rival: Adequate provision with refusal could also yield low coverage
test.discriminating_observation: Local records of stock availability, staff visits and refusal under the same rule
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S02 explicitly contrasts mandate with resource limits and easier institutional reach; no comparable district data supplied
test.remaining_ambiguity: Capacity constraints supported, relative contribution against distrust unmeasured.

statement: The 1885 Ottoman rules conditioned school entry and state-linked roles on vaccination evidence; later rules enlarged obligations and penalties, so legally induced uptake cannot be equated with consent.

sources.supports: Specific conditions, fines and certification rules.

counterevidence: The same source reports incomplete enforcement and implementation.
inference_limits: Legal exposure is not evidence of actual penalties or every household's inability to evade.

test.reason: Documents compulsion instruments and the logical limit of inferring consent from compliance.

statement: Lister’s 1867 address presented an evolving wound-treatment practice through cases and claimed ward improvements, rather than a controlled trial of a fixed protocol.

sources.locator: Opening clinical discussion; paragraph beginning If the severest forms; concluding ward discussion
sources.supports: Procedural adaptations, case reports and asserted outcomes.

counterevidence: Observations can be informative despite lacking controlled identification.
inference_limits: Does not deny antisepsis efficacy or validate every claim in Lister's address.

test.reason: Characterizes the evidence form and treatment specification in the historical document.

statement: Contemporary objections to Lister’s aggregate outcome comparisons included small samples, case comparability and hospital epidemic cycles, making simple before/after attribution contestable.

sources.locator: Statistics; Glasgow Royal Infirmary; Longer-term perspective
sources.supports: Examines selection periods, small numbers and changing background mortality.

counterevidence: Improvement in fracture management and other outcomes may still support antiseptic benefits.
inference_limits: Hamilton reconstruction is mediated through Tröhler; no independent raw-data reanalysis.

test.mechanism_chain: Chosen comparison periods -> apparent mortality reduction -> efficacy inference
test.strongest_rival: Epidemic cycles, selection and case mix can produce a similar comparison
test.discriminating_observation: Longer ward series, comparable operations and independent comparison wards
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S05 reports wide prior fluctuation and very small operation counts, weakening the simple inference
test.remaining_ambiguity: Does not separate all genuine treatment effects from confounding; critiques are not proof of no benefit.

statement: Demonstration, detailed instruction and embodied operative skills contributed to communicating Listerian practice; adoption was not reducible to assent to germ theory.

sources.supports: Traces demonstrations, hands-on details, students and adaptation.

counterevidence: Reputation, materials and institutional differences could explain the same diffusion pattern.
inference_limits: No controlled comparison isolates training from selection of motivated trainees.

test.mechanism_chain: New multi-step regimen -> demonstration and practice -> ability to reproduce treatment
test.strongest_rival: Prestige and self-selection of adherents may explain following the same teachers
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable surgeons with and without direct training, measured performance rather than declared allegiance
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S04 documents channels and adaptations but does not supply such matched outcomes
test.remaining_ambiguity: Contribution is plausible and documented; necessity or magnitude not identified.

statement: Alsan and Goldin estimate that combined safe water and effective sewerage account for about one-third of the decline in log under-five mortality in their jointly treated Massachusetts municipalities, 1880–1920; the interventions are complementary in their preferred model.

sources.supports: Staggered completion design and reported decomposition of 26.6 out of 79.2 log points.

counterevidence: Other sanitary improvements, spillovers and population selection could threaten the design.
inference_limits: Local estimate under model assumptions; neither a universal effect nor the national mortality contribution.

test.mechanism_chain: Combined exposure-route interventions -> reduced pathogen exposure -> lower child mortality
test.strongest_rival: Other changes or selective migration timed with construction could mimic the effect
test.discriminating_observation: No pre-trend divergence, age/cause specificity and stable composition around completion
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S06 reports pre-trend checks, age/cause contrasts, Table 4 composition checks and robustness
test.remaining_ambiguity: Observational identification remains conditional; engineering rollout not random assignment.

statement: Regional compulsory participation and payment formed part of the Massachusetts sewerage response to pollution crossing municipal boundaries.

sources.supports: Upstream/downstream problem and legally coordinated regional system.

counterevidence: Voluntary bargains or private coordination might have supplied a viable alternative.
inference_limits: No claim that compulsion was uniquely necessary, consensual or costlessly beneficial.

test.mechanism_chain: Cross-boundary sewage costs -> regional obligations -> coordinated investment
test.strongest_rival: Political influence or voluntary coordination could deliver similar investment
test.discriminating_observation: Evidence of failed voluntary arrangements and subsequent contribution changes under mandate
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S06 documents boundary problem and mandate; not a counterfactual comparison of governance regimes
test.remaining_ambiguity: Observed institutional route does not prove necessity.

statement: The size of clean-water contributions to aggregate US mortality decline remains disputed across analyses using overlapping records and different coding choices.

sources.supports: Smaller estimates and sensitivity to transcription, dates and denominators.
Defends substantial total effect while acknowledging reduced infant estimate and coding differences.

counterevidence: The disagreement does not erase agreement that filtration reduced typhoid mortality.
inference_limits: Final-paper data and reply not audited; MED-S08 abstract cannot adjudicate calculations.

test.mechanism_chain: Record coding and intervention timing -> different panel estimates -> different historical attribution
test.strongest_rival: Real treatment heterogeneity across cities could also explain differences
test.discriminating_observation: Reestimate with harmonized raw counts, population and partial-year rules
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S07 reports within-data corrections; MED-S08 attributes remaining difference to coding and denominators
test.remaining_ambiguity: No independent replication here; shared data means source count is not independent corroboration.

statement: Wartime penicillin supply required solving culture-yield and downstream-processing problems in addition to establishing clinical promise.

sources.supports: Scale-up, extraction, purification and sterile production.
Culture medium and strain work.

counterevidence: Institutional accounts may overstate their own component's contribution.
inference_limits: Process-specific contribution, not proof that this exact route was the only possible route.

test.mechanism_chain: Low usable yield -> strain/media/process work -> more recoverable output
test.strongest_rival: Expansion of vessel numbers or different extraction routes might explain part of output growth
test.discriminating_observation: Measured yields and losses before/after controlled process changes
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S09/S10 describe process improvements and production transition; no primary batch logs inspected
test.remaining_ambiguity: Causal weights and alternative industrial routes remain unresolved.

statement: Pfizer’s prior submerged-fermentation experience was an identified contributor to its penicillin production route.

sources.supports: Connects gluconic-acid process knowledge to penicillin tanks.

counterevidence: Capital, procurement access and new staff might matter as much as inherited skills.
inference_limits: Company-centred retrospective; not a cross-firm estimate or universal prerequisite.

test.mechanism_chain: Prior fermentation know-how -> adaptation of tanks/sterility controls -> production scale-up
test.strongest_rival: Capital and purchasing incentives could account for success despite different prior experience
test.discriminating_observation: Compare firms with similar finance and different inherited fermentation capabilities
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S09 names a concrete technical transfer; no matched firm histories examined
test.remaining_ambiguity: Source may organize history retrospectively around eventual success.

statement: Governmental coordination and firms’ investment choices accompanied penicillin scale-up, while committing plant capacity involved opportunity costs.

sources.locator: Opening; Penicillin Production by Deep-tank Fermentation
sources.supports: Government approach to firms and risk of curtailing other products.
Public laboratory/industrial connection.

counterevidence: Rising private expectations of demand might have induced investment without equivalent coordination.
inference_limits: No procurement-contract audit or cost-benefit estimate.

test.mechanism_chain: Wartime demand and public coordination -> commitments to risky capacity -> enlarged supply
test.strongest_rival: Private expected profitability could independently cause the investment
test.discriminating_observation: Dated contracts, capacity plans and internal investment deliberations
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S09/S10 document collaboration and resource commitment, not the counterfactual financing path
test.remaining_ambiguity: Correlation with wartime effort does not establish unique necessity.

statement: Sri Lankan records reported six indigenous and eleven imported malaria cases in 1963, followed by reduced control activity and a major late-1960s resurgence.

sources.locator: Malaria in Sri Lanka During the Second Half of the Twentieth Century
sources.supports: Counts and programme sequence.

sources.locator: Weakening of the malaria control programme, Sri Lanka paragraph
sources.supports: Same sequence with surveillance and population-movement qualifications.

counterevidence: Both accounts inherit overlapping historical records.
inference_limits: Case counts depend on detection; sequence alone is not a causal estimate.

test.reason: Records temporal pattern and reported classifications without allocating causal shares.

statement: The inspected chronology does not justify attributing Sri Lanka’s initial late-1960s reversal solely to DDT resistance: relaxation began earlier, while the account dates emerging resistance to 1969. The account reports replacement of DDT by malathion in 1977.

sources.locator: Second Half of the Twentieth Century
sources.supports: 1964 consolidation, later resurgence, 1969 resistance and 1977 replacement.

sources.locator: Sri Lanka example and Technical problems
sources.supports: Multiple operational and ecological causes.

counterevidence: Resistance may have been present before detection and can interact with weakened operations.
inference_limits: Rejects a sole-cause assertion; does not establish absence of earlier resistance or a unique alternative cause.

test.mechanism_chain: Operational relaxation before reported resistance -> reduced suppression -> renewed transmission
test.strongest_rival: Undetected earlier resistance could also contribute
test.discriminating_observation: Contemporaneous susceptibility assays and local coverage preceding resurgence
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S11 chronology and MED-S12 multi-factor narrative inspected; first causal claim fails temporal sufficiency
test.remaining_ambiguity: Detection lag and intertwined ecological changes remain unresolved.

statement: WHO announced Sri Lanka’s malaria-free certification in September 2016 after three consecutive years of documented zero transmission.

sources.supports: Dated public certification announcement and qualification period.

counterevidence: Certification relies on programme surveillance and is not proof of zero imported infections.
inference_limits: Historical certification only; no statement about present-day status.

test.reason: Dated official event with precisely bounded meaning.

statement: Cohen et al. catalogued 75 malaria resurgence events; causes were reported attributions, and only 16% of suggested causes had substantial supporting analysis.

sources.supports: Review denominators and evidence grading.

counterevidence: Review may miss undocumented events and attribution reflects authors' interests.
inference_limits: Counts cannot estimate causal frequency or compare event magnitude.

test.reason: Describes review construction and its own evidence limits.

statement: The 1971 refugee-camp implementation led by Mahalanabis demonstrated family-administered oral rehydration in an emergency, extending evidence beyond tightly staffed research settings.

sources.supports: Contrasts refugee-camp administration by families with Matlab monitoring.

counterevidence: Emergency adoption may not predict routine household use or comparative efficacy.
inference_limits: Original camp report not independently audited; historical account relies partly on participants.

test.mechanism_chain: Emergency scarcity of clinical labour -> caregiver administration -> feasible delivery outside intensive monitoring
test.strongest_rival: Only unusually selected patients/families may have made the demonstration feasible
test.discriminating_observation: Observed use with less professional supervision under actual camp conditions
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S13 explicitly contrasts staffing and administration; supports operational feasibility in that setting
test.remaining_ambiguity: Does not establish universal substitution for clinical care or later diffusion effect.

statement: BRAC’s 1980s programme used household demonstration, monitoring and wider community engagement; its 1993 evaluation sampled 90 villages from three programme phases. Teaching coexisted with expanding packaged-ORS distribution.

sources.supports: Teaching approach, worker monitoring and survey design.

counterevidence: Programme-affiliated evaluation and informal transmission complicate attribution.
inference_limits: Reach, retained competence, reported use and health outcomes remain separate measures.

test.reason: Describes intervention organization and sample, not causal programme efficacy.

statement: Chowdhury et al. Table 2 reports 51.8%, 54.5% and 53.0% ORT use for all reported diarrhoeal episodes across cohorts; the abstract’s 60% conflicts with that denominator, while the discussion obtains over 60% after excluding dysentery.

sources.locator: p. 58 abstract; p. 62 Table 2 footnote; pp. 64–65 Discussion
sources.supports: Direct denominator comparison; broad ORT definition includes home fluids.

counterevidence: The abstract could reflect an unstated restriction rather than a transcription error.
inference_limits: Not strict packaged-ORS coverage or population-weighted national rate; no new pooled estimate calculated.

test.reason: Source-internal measurement audit, verified against table and discussion rather than abstract alone.

statement: In experiment 1 of the 2011–2012 one-city Chinese audit, expected purchase outside the hospital reduced antibiotic prescribing from 55% to 10% without a request; with a request, the corresponding rates were 85% and 14%.

sources.supports: Randomly assigned standardized-patient roles and reported encounter rates.

counterevidence: Scripts may signal factors besides lost revenue; auditors were not blinded.
inference_limits: Identifies response to scripts in this sample, not national policy effects or patient health effects.

test.mechanism_chain: Changed expected dispensing location -> changed provider incentives/signals -> prescribing response
test.strongest_rival: Outside-purchase script may signal offense, distrust or counterfeit risk
test.discriminating_observation: Demand held explicit while purchase location changes; further scripts varying alternative signals
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S15 paired physician design and second-experiment scripts inspected; demand effect largely disappears with outside purchase
test.remaining_ambiguity: Mechanism decomposition less secure than treatment-script effect.

statement: The audit’s additional scripts support financial incentives as a major explanation for prescribing in its sampled encounters, while leaving general-equilibrium reform effects unresolved.

sources.supports: Relative-pharmacy, knowledge and gift treatments test rival interpretations.

counterevidence: Social signaling cannot be removed perfectly; providers may substitute other services after reform.
inference_limits: Not an estimate of nationwide incentive removal or a complete explanation of prescribing everywhere.

test.mechanism_chain: Revenue expectation -> unnecessary prescription incentive -> observed excess use
test.strongest_rival: Etiquette, perceived demand and drug-quality concern predict some similar responses
test.discriminating_observation: Changing those signals while maintaining outside-purchase condition
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S15 reports persistence under relative-pharmacy script and smaller knowledge effects; original experiment examined
test.remaining_ambiguity: Alternative signals remain bundled and actual reforms change hospital budgets.

statement: This prescribing experiment illustrates a possible divergence between provider revenue and appropriate use, but does not quantify resulting antimicrobial resistance or total social harm.

sources.supports: Revenue mechanism, concern about resistance and measured prescribing outcome.

counterevidence: Needed treatment can also be underprovided, and prescription does not prove ingestion.
inference_limits: Externality is a mechanism-level interpretation, not a measured outcome of these visits.

test.mechanism_chain: Revenue incentive -> unnecessary antibiotic exposure if prescriptions used -> possible wider resistance cost
test.strongest_rival: Prescriptions may not be used or marginal ecological effects may be small in a given setting
test.discriminating_observation: Link actual dispensed use to resistance outcomes with appropriate controls
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S15 establishes encounter prescribing responses but collected no resistance outcomes
test.remaining_ambiguity: Private incentive divergence supported; ecological magnitude and welfare balance unmeasured.

statement: ORBIS models Roman connectivity as a seasonally variable combination of road, river and sea routes; its route outputs are modeled opportunities rather than observed adoption or actual journeys.

sources.supports: Authors define average structural simulations, seasonal constraints and non-contemporaneous road coverage.

counterevidence: Local knowledge, secondary roads and route-specific hazards can change actual decisions.
inference_limits: A network model cannot establish traffic shares, willingness to adopt, welfare or the causal contribution of Roman state road building.

test.reason: Bounded documentary/model/measurement statement; does not itself estimate a causal contribution. Associated causal propositions are tested separately.

statement: For pottery movement in lowland Britain c. 250–400 CE, Wiseman and colleagues infer best-fit road costs roughly three times river and four times sea costs, with wide uncertainty and regional river variation.

sources.supports: Estimated ratios are derived from excavated pottery distributions and a transport network.

counterevidence: Text-based Mediterranean estimates can imply much greater water advantages; the authors argue these often compare unlike segments and omit handling costs.
inference_limits: Rural pottery distribution, not all goods or military movement; the cost-demand model, sample and inferred routes matter. Abstract and conclusion summarize river ranges differently; no precise interval is generalized here.

test.mechanism_chain: Transport/transfer costs vary by mode -> buyers face different delivered costs -> pottery demand declines with generalized distance -> observed distribution fits moderate modal ratios.
test.strongest_rival: Institutional supply, product preference or distribution hubs generate the same spatial decay without the assumed cost-demand relationship.
test.discriminating_observation: Independent consignment/freight accounts or repeated fits across commodities and regions with different social distributions would separate general costs from pottery-specific institutions.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read MOB-S02 §1.1, Table 3 and §§4.4–5: fits, river variation and rural/military exclusions support a bounded inference, not direct traffic measurement.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cost is inferred from the outcome to be explained; network and demand assumptions leave multiple explanations possible.

statement: Segment-level freight prices can misstate door-to-door modal advantages when transshipment, storage, port charges and access legs are omitted.

sources.supports: Explicit chain of transport costs and critique of comparisons omitting transfers.
ORBIS warns expense data are schematic and uses a price-edict sailing-time calibration.

counterevidence: Long bulk sea voyages can retain a large advantage despite transfer costs.
inference_limits: This is a measurement/mechanism proposition; it does not imply Roman land transport was universally cheaper or universally preferred.

test.mechanism_chain: Additional transfers/access legs incur resources -> total delivery cost differs from line-haul price -> ranking inferred from a segment may change.
test.strongest_rival: Sea advantages remain dominant because transfer costs are negligible relative to long line-haul savings.
test.discriminating_observation: Observe or reconstruct full chains at different distances; whether adding transfers changes relative delivered cost distinguishes claims for a particular route.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S02 explicitly enumerates omitted costs and derives different end-to-end ratios; MOB-S01 acknowledges schematic price calibration.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The existence of omitted terms is established, but no universal ranking reversal is demonstrated.

statement: Inka expansion incorporated earlier Andean routes and added or maintained roads, stores and wayside facilities, so imperial scaling was partly the integration of inherited infrastructure.

sources.locator: printed pp. 321 and 324–325, Description and History
sources.supports: Lists road engineering and supply structures and states that much of the network preceded Inka occupation.

counterevidence: The evaluation also describes new secondary roads; inheritance does not mean no technical innovation or expansion.
inference_limits: Heritage synthesis, not a dated census of every route. No single inventor or uniform date of network completion is assigned.

test.reason: Bounded documentary/model/measurement statement; does not itself estimate a causal contribution. Associated causal propositions are tested separately.

statement: For Garrido’s Cachiyuyo de Llampos road segment in the Atacama, water and forage scarcity make predominantly pedestrian traffic more plausible than regular llama caravans.

sources.supports: Survey geography, scarce water, absent vegetation and alternative highland pasture routes motivate the author’s inference.

counterevidence: Llama transport occurred elsewhere in the Andes; occasional camelid use on this segment is not excluded.
inference_limits: Traffic composition is inferred, not counted. This supports ecological task differentiation rather than a claim that Inka roads generally lacked pack-animal traffic.

test.mechanism_chain: Sparse water/forage -> higher logistical burden for llama caravans -> travelers favor pedestrian traffic on this segment.
test.strongest_rival: Organized supply or small occasional caravans allowed substantial pack-animal traffic despite local scarcity.
test.discriminating_observation: Road-associated corrals, dung, feed provision or transport-specific evidence would discriminate better than generic camelid food bones.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S04 §4.1 reports ecology, limited water and absent ethnographic caravan precedent for this locality; no transport census was found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Ecological feasibility and alternative-route reasoning do not establish actual traffic shares; preservation/recognition of animal evidence must be tested.
