statement: At Cachiyuyo de Llampos, settlement, craft and roadside assemblages support Garrido’s interpretation that some local miners used the Inka Road for exchange beyond directly administered state production.

sources.supports: Mining camps concentrated nearer the road; non-Inka roadside craft activity and contrast with official Tambo Medanoso inform the interpretation.

counterevidence: Substantial state-controlled mining and corvée systems existed in other locations discussed by the same author.
inference_limits: Absence of elite architecture is not proof of wholly autonomous exchange; site chronology, informal supervision and local intermediaries remain alternatives.

statement: Early private Indian railway expansion combined British capital with colonial guarantees, while government line-placement priorities included military control; observed construction was not simply a market vote by passengers or farmers.

sources.supports: Concession contracts and 5% capital guarantee at a fixed exchange rate; payments when returns fell short.
Government line placement and military priorities using historical planning documents.
Guarantee shortfalls were funded from Government of India tax revenues.

inference_limits: Historians’ reconstructions of planning and contracts, not independent inspection here of every concession or Dalhousie minute. No claim that all lines had identical motives.

test.mechanism_chain: Risky capital project and colonial strategic priorities -> guaranteed concessions and state routing -> financed trunk-line deployment.

test.discriminating_observation: Comparable unguaranteed proposals, financing failures and decision correspondence predating construction would help separate risk support from redundant subsidy.

test.remaining_ambiguity: Unmeasured service quality and other organizational changes may matter; worker welfare cannot be inferred from firm costs.

test.mechanism_chain: Trained operators and capital reach a place with customers -> workshop established -> local printing deployment
test.strongest_rival: Demand or city size alone attracts presses; apparent skill networks merely follow profitable locations.
test.discriminating_observation: Large nonadopting cities and adoption varying with technical-network proximity after demand controls; workshop correspondence would be stronger.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S09 records forty of the hundred largest cities without a press and discusses printer mobility, financial requirements and distance.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Demand, skills and funding are jointly selected; historical sequencing and IV assumptions do not fully separate them.

statement: In Dittmar and Seabold's European printing-city analysis, local competition is associated with lower book prices and changes in publication output; transport costs make location consequential even after technical feasibility.

sources.supports: Book-price evidence, printer entry/death strategy, transport and local market structure.

counterevidence: Competition, customer demand and content can influence one another; death also disrupts expertise and relationships.
inference_limits: Effects conditional on identification assumptions. Prices are from a selected purchasing record; editions are not copies sold or readers.

test.mechanism_chain: Entry or disrupted collusion -> increased local competition -> changed prices and content
test.strongest_rival: Growing demand drives entry and output, or printer death changes scarce expertise directly rather than competition.
test.discriminating_observation: Prices/output shifting with death-induced competitive changes rather than only growing markets; direct skill-channel tests.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S10 compares entries/exits and printer deaths, uses Colón purchase prices and finds lower prices with more local printers; §3 notes different death measures and selection.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Exclusion restriction is substantive; a death can alter more than market structure. This is evidence from the authors' design, not an independent replication.

statement: Studies of early European printing estimate city-growth and content effects using distance from Mainz and printer deaths as instruments; interpretation as causal depends on excluding other geography, expertise and network channels.

sources.locator: §V.E, pp. 1157–63, IV design and comparison with OLS
sources.supports: Distance instrument and tests, outcome is city population growth.
Printer-death designs for competition/content and outcomes.

counterevidence: Pre-trend and control checks support the studies, but exclusion cannot be established by chronology alone; city growth can involve redistribution by migration.
inference_limits: Do not treat city population as national productivity, welfare or a universal print effect. Designs share scholarship and some data foundations.

test.mechanism_chain: Local printing/content access -> useful skills or ideological transmission -> observed city or institutional outcome
test.strongest_rival: Underlying commercial growth or institutions cause both printing and outcomes; geography/deaths affect outcomes through other channels.
test.discriminating_observation: Adoption/output shocks unrelated to pre-trends, sector-specific effects, and falsification of direct channels.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S09 checks prior growth and uses Mainz distance; NET-S10 uses content-specific printer-death variation. Historical production and controls were inspected; estimates not re-estimated.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No independent replication; validity remains conditional and external validity does not extend automatically to other book cultures.

statement: Schwartz finds no inspected original of the alleged Bayezid II/Selim I general printing bans, while the extant 1588 firman protects merchants selling printed Arabic books; a blanket ban is not established evidence.

sources.locator: pp. 6–7, The Non-Extant Firmans and The First Extant Firman; pp. 19–26 on inherited accounts
sources.supports: Documentary contrast and lineage of repeated ban claims.

counterevidence: Absence of these documents does not establish universal permission; narrower restrictions and enforcement could exist.
inference_limits: Claim concerns evidential support for alleged blanket bans, not proof that no Ottoman restrictions ever occurred.

test.mechanism_chain: Proposed general ban -> suppression of printing/trade -> limited uptake
test.strongest_rival: Later writers conflated specific restrictions or preferences into a general ban; permission varied by actor and text.
test.discriminating_observation: An authentic general prohibitory decree or consistent enforcement records versus extant permissions predating 1727.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S11 traces repeated assertions without an original decree and closely reads the 1588 protective firman.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Archival loss remains possible; extant permission defeats a timeless blanket claim but not all narrower prohibitions.

statement: The 1727 grant to Müteferrika permitted particular printing subjects and required learned correctors through the associated fatwa; it both enabled a project and delimited its scope.

sources.locator: pp. 9–11, Ahmed III firman and quoted fatwa
sources.supports: Named permission, subject exclusions and appointment of correctors.

counterevidence: The documents do not state every motive for excluding religious subjects or prove a previous universal prohibition.
inference_limits: Regulatory design establishes permitted scope, not the effectiveness of correction or its impact on sales.

test.mechanism_chain: Petition and expertise claim -> religious/legal approval with correction and subject conditions -> authorised press project
test.strongest_rival: Approval merely formalises an independently viable venture; exclusions reflect broader suppression rather than quality or requested scope.
test.discriminating_observation: Text of the grant/fatwa and actual correcting practices; counterfactual applications denied without conditions.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S11 pp. 9–11 reproduces the permitted subjects and correction condition, and notes the request's own exclusions.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Permit text supports formal enabling/limitation, but cannot identify motives, compliance or marginal commercial effect.

statement: Sabev reports 8,200 initial copies across thirteen editions with known runs, estimates three other runs, and records 2,981 remaining copies in Müteferrika's estate; stock subtraction is not a directly observed sales measure.

sources.supports: Known/assumed runs, estate stock, gifts, different finishing and market exposure.

counterevidence: Large residual stock is consistent with slow sales; earlier titles had more years available and gifts removed copies without sales.
inference_limits: Author's edition grouping and reconstructed figures retained; original register not recounted. No exact profit, sell-through or readership rate.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: Sabev finds Müteferrika prints in sixteen of 335 selected Istanbul askeri probate inventories with more than three books, dated 1724–1748; some owners were religious functionaries.

sources.supports: Selection rules, 335 inventories, sixteen containing prints, religious-functionary owners and stated caveats.

counterevidence: Probates omit living ownership, gifts, donations and readers who borrowed; surviving registers and askeri status select the sample.
inference_limits: High confidence in author's stated result, not independent archive replication. Not a population adoption or literacy denominator.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: In the northern Indian Ocean routes described by fifteenth-/sixteenth-century navigation texts, knowledge of regional and transitional winds mattered within the broad monsoon pattern; season was part of route selection.

sources.supports: Regional wind windows, departure times and route instructions.

counterevidence: Different routes had different windows; general environment does not by itself determine mariners' choices or voyage outcomes.
inference_limits: No fleet-level timing distribution, failure rate or comparison of trained/untrained crews is available.

test.mechanism_chain: Route-specific seasonal knowledge -> chosen departure/bearing -> use of favourable winds and avoidance of hazards
test.strongest_rival: The general monsoon cycle alone suffices; detailed pilot knowledge adds little.
test.discriminating_observation: Instructions distinguishing routes and transitional windows within the same broad season; voyage outcomes would test magnitude.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S13 identifies countervailing winds and an eastward Bay of Bengal window, and reports route-specific dates and hazards.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Detailed prescriptions show relevant distinctions but not actual compliance or a quantified safety benefit.

statement: Staples describes wooden star-altitude aids and magnetic compasses using stellar direction names in late medieval Indian Ocean navigation; Tolmacheva calls magnetic use rare, leaving carriage prevalence unmeasured.

sources.locator: §3 p. 4, fingers, wooden instruments and stellar rhumb names
sources.supports: Layering of standardising instruments and established direction conventions.

sources.locator: paragraph beginning Where the Chinese compass had 28 rhumbs
sources.supports: Stellar compass scheme and assertion of rare magnetic-compass use.

counterevidence: The two sources share underlying texts and differ in emphasis on prevalence; a stellar compass is a directional scheme, not necessarily a magnetic device.
inference_limits: No claim that all ships used compasses, that wooden instruments had a quantified accuracy, or that later kamal descriptions reproduce all earlier instruments.

test.mechanism_chain: Familiar stellar conventions plus measuring aids -> integration with existing navigation skills -> hybrid operating system
test.strongest_rival: An imported magnetic device substitutes for stellar/local knowledge and becomes a universal prerequisite.
test.discriminating_observation: Documents retaining stellar nomenclature and methods alongside devices; actual equipment inventories for prevalence.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S13 records integration of stellar names into magnetic directions and wooden measurement; NET-S14 reports rare compass carriage.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Textual prescription is not fleet practice; both scholars rely heavily on the same navigational corpus. Prevalence remains unresolved.

statement: Ibn Majid's surviving instructions include verse suitable for memorisation and lack associated maps, while Portuguese reports describe some Indian Ocean chart use; absence in one corpus does not establish universal chartlessness.

sources.locator: paragraphs beginning It appears that early Portuguese sailors, Curiously, and Moreover
sources.supports: Contrasting chart evidence and verse sailing instructions.
Difference between Arabic literary references and Portuguese testimony; limitations of editions/translations.

counterevidence: Charts may have existed but not survived; verse need not prove every navigator memorised it.
inference_limits: No chart adoption rate or causal effect of oral transmission; inherited corpus is not an exhaustive census of practice.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: The anonymous 1498 voyage narrative reports da Gama seizing a Malindi court servant while demanding pilots, then receiving a pilot and departing with him on 24 April; this documents local expertise and coercion in one crossing episode.

sources.locator: pp. 45–47, Malindi entry for 22 April and Across the Gulf entry for 24 April 1498
sources.supports: Hostage seizure, pilot provision and departure with that pilot.

counterevidence: Narrator's religious identification is unreliable; this single episode does not show the pilot's full role or whether the coercion was necessary.
inference_limits: Do not identify the pilot as Ibn Majid, infer all local recruitment was coerced, or use one voyage as a safety/accuracy comparison.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: Kyselka’s contemporaneous account records Hōkūleʻa’s 1980 Hawaiʻi–Tahiti return voyage under Nainoa Thompson’s non-instrument navigation, with planetarium training, Mau Piailug’s teaching and escort-based documentation explicitly present.

sources.supports: Training, successful landfall and return, twice-daily position reports and instrument comparison.

counterevidence: This was a supported modern voyage, not a controlled recreation of every ancient condition.
inference_limits: Demonstrates this configuration’s operation; no proof of a particular ancient migration, population uptake or cargo economics.

test.reason: Reports a specific documented voyage and its stated supports, not their separate causal effect.

statement: The 1979–1980 apprenticeship and March 2007 Satawal initiation support an intergenerational, inter-island knowledge-transmission pathway in voyaging renewal; they do not establish that one navigator alone caused a Pacific-wide cultural revival.

sources.supports: Direct learning from Mau and planetarium practice.
Eleven Satawal and five Hawaiʻi initiates and responsibility to perpetuate knowledge.

counterevidence: PVS accounts also celebrate many canoe builders and participants; institution and eyewitness source share a network.
inference_limits: Formal initiation is neither a census of practicing navigators nor a standardized competence test.

test.mechanism_chain: Experienced navigator agrees to teach -> repeated sea and classroom practice -> new navigators operate and receive recognition
test.strongest_rival: Museum science, organizational support and a wider cultural movement independently sustain revival; these may complement teaching
test.discriminating_observation: Training sequence and autonomous voyages by multiple pupils, with explicit instructional histories rather than just shared symbols
test.evidence_sought_found: S01 traces instruction before the 1980 voyage; S03 identifies later pupils and ceremony
test.remaining_ambiguity: No comparison of equally supported trainees without this teaching; many inputs co-varied

statement: PVS records a 1978 capsize and loss of Eddie Aikau, followed by renewed voyages including 1980; revival included severe operational failure, not an uninterrupted sequence of successful demonstrations.

sources.locator: Tragedy and A Generation of Renewal sections
sources.supports: 1978 capsize, rescue/loss, resumption in 1980.

counterevidence: Retrospective narrative emphasizes perseverance.
inference_limits: Does not identify the capsize’s technical cause or quantify safety changes or a voyage failure rate.

test.reason: Bounded chronology of failure and resumption.

statement: Wilson-Hokowhitu’s interviews with women voyagers document ancestral responsibility and identity as expressed reasons for participation, alongside sacrifices of volunteer time; several interviewees declined or did not know personal genealogies.

sources.supports: Interview method, participants’ choice about genealogy, volunteering and expressed motivations.

counterevidence: Interview framing explicitly invited genealogical and spiritual reflection.
inference_limits: Purposive qualitative evidence cannot establish prevalence, an exclusive motive, equal entry or wage effects; spiritual accounts are recorded as participants’ interpretations.

test.reason: Direct self-reports about purpose and participation barriers; no causal productivity claim.

statement: At Muldoons Trap Complex, sediment stratigraphy and AMS charcoal dates support an early excavated channel around 6,600 cal BP and a later wall-building episode around 600–800 cal BP, with an intervening hiatus.

sources.supports: Dated fill, mixed horizon, proposed construction sequence.

counterevidence: Fluvial charcoal can be redeposited or have inherited age; investigators explicitly address these problems.
inference_limits: One excavated feature does not date every trap, establish continuous operation, or measure the regional share of food supplied.

test.reason: Summarizes authors’ site-specific chronological interpretation, not a first-invention or continuous-use claim.

statement: Tae Rak’s enlarged drainage works, completed in 1954 despite recorded opposition, sharply curtailed the water conditions for lake-margin trapping; this was institutional and hydrological disabling rather than a demonstrated voluntary choice of a more productive fishery.

sources.supports: Opposition, drainage, short water retention and traps rarely functioning outside floods.
Drain completion in 1954 and later restoration attempts.

counterevidence: Drainage served pastoral flood-control and grazing objectives; those benefits are not evaluated here.
inference_limits: Underlying engineering measurements and original opposition letters not acquired. Sources share project lineage.

test.mechanism_chain: Pastoral drainage authorized over objections -> rapid loss of retained lake water -> trap operating windows shrink
test.strongest_rival: Fishing fell because tastes, labor allocation or alternative livelihoods changed, independently of drainage
test.discriminating_observation: Operation varies with retained water and flood episodes; objections show fishing decline was not simply revealed preference
test.evidence_sought_found: S05 describes rapid recession and flood-only functioning; S06 records failed/restored water-control attempts
test.remaining_ambiguity: No catch time series; labor and ecological change can operate alongside water loss

statement: The 2010 cultural weir restored retained water under a negotiated 52.4 m AHD setting intended to limit flooding of upstream farms; the nomination says this could reactivate most trap complexes but excluded Muldoons at that level.

sources.supports: 2010 restoration, selected water level and differing trap reach.
Failed early trial, planning, hydrological studies, land return and construction.

counterevidence: Restoration also relied on heavy rainfall; the weir was not sufficient by itself.
inference_limits: Not proof that all potentially wetted traps were operated or that precolonial output returned.

test.mechanism_chain: Land return and negotiated engineering -> water retention compatible with neighboring property constraints -> uneven hydraulic reactivation
test.strongest_rival: Rainfall alone restored the lake, with formal restoration incidental
test.discriminating_observation: Retention duration before/after at comparable inflow, and trap elevation relative to negotiated water setting
test.evidence_sought_found: S05 explains selection of level and excluded complex; S06 documents failed trial and successive studies
test.remaining_ambiguity: Matched hydrological time series not acquired; rainfall and gate management interact

statement: Gunditj Mirring reports supported Aboriginal recruitment, training and supervision during January–May 2010 weir construction, including construction and some administrative work.

sources.supports: Government employment support and specific task opportunities.

counterevidence: Implementer account may foreground programme successes.
inference_limits: No employee count, wage, duration beyond construction, retention or distributional impact is reported.

test.reason: Records a specified employment/training programme without inferring household prosperity.

statement: The 2000s Martu studies observe hunting-related burning within a contemporary mixed economy that includes vehicle travel and purchased food; they do not observe an unchanged precolonial regime.

sources.supports: Outstation return, vehicle-supported foraging and stores.
347 sample days, 1,811 bouts and 104 foragers, 2000–2010.

counterevidence: Site use is spatially selective and does not represent all Martu territory.
inference_limits: No estimate of the share of all households practicing burning or its ancient form.

test.reason: Defines actual observed users and configuration.

statement: The 2008 study reports higher mean winter small-game hunting returns with burning than without (656 versus 478 edible kcal/hour), with 152 burning and 89 non-burning hunts; assignment was observational.

sources.supports: Hunt sample sizes, harvest, return-rate and failure comparisons.

counterevidence: Hunters choose when and where to burn; hunting skill and patch condition can differ across groups.
inference_limits: These are foraging-return observations, not wages or a randomized treatment effect.

test.reason: A within-study association with a stated outcome and comparator; no unqualified claim that burning caused the difference.

statement: In the 1999–2010 study region, zones classified as Martu-burning dominated had smaller and more clustered fires and weaker rainfall-related fire-size expansion than lightning-dominated zones; this challenges a climate-only account for these landscapes.

sources.supports: Fire-size comparison, antecedent-rainfall test, mapped regime definition and ground truth.

counterevidence: Ignitions are proxied by tracks/community distance, and landscape selection is nonrandom. The seasonal fraction burnt did not differ significantly.
inference_limits: No automatic generalization to forests, other Indigenous burning systems, extinction rates or total ecological welfare.

test.mechanism_chain: Repeated small hunting fires -> nearby patches at different fuel ages -> breaks limit spread under rainfall-driven fuel accumulation
test.strongest_rival: Climate and substrate alone explain fire patterns; settled/tracked areas occupy different environments
test.discriminating_observation: Different rainfall–fire-size relations within comparable vegetation and across seasons, plus direct burning observations
test.evidence_sought_found: S08 compares regimes and climate interaction in spinifex country and reports field observations; 90% ground-truth accuracy on 50 track-accessible points
test.remaining_ambiguity: Proxy classification, unmeasured local environment and track access remain confounds

statement: The Martu evidence supports a feedback hypothesis in which immediate small-game foraging benefits help maintain repeated burns and landscape heterogeneity without requiring a central planner to direct every ignition.

sources.supports: Task-specific burning benefits and localized landscape response.

sources.locator: Materials and Methods, Martu burning behavior
sources.supports: Gendered task differences, mobility and resulting fire patterns.

counterevidence: Kin obligations, cultural authority and longer-term ecological aims can coexist with immediate benefits; no absence of institutions is claimed.
inference_limits: Does not establish selfish optimization, universal stewardship, or sufficient incentives under new conditions.

test.mechanism_chain: Task-level returns and skilled decisions -> repeated spatially patterned ignitions -> locally maintained mosaic -> further foraging benefits
test.strongest_rival: Burning is maintained principally by norms or intentional collective stewardship; returns correlate with practices but are not decisive
test.discriminating_observation: Task-specific adoption variation, expressed decisions and changes in burning when immediate returns change
test.evidence_sought_found: S07 finds burning concentrated in small-game hunting and no comparable immediate return gain for large-game burning; S08 maps the spatial association
test.remaining_ambiguity: No experiment on motivations or norms; compatible mechanisms remain

statement: Kuk’s published sequence differentiates mounded cultivation around 6,950–6,440 cal BP from ditch cultivation beginning around 4,350–3,980 cal BP; a later account maps multiple, locally varying Phase 3 ditch configurations.

sources.supports: Different phase dates and feature forms.
Phase 3 networks, variable spatial use and earlier possible linear experiments.

counterevidence: Dating boundaries are approximate; only excavated or exposed traces survive.
inference_limits: Not a regional diffusion curve, proof of centralized command or a global independent-invention verdict.

test.reason: Describes a local chronological and material distinction.

statement: Kuk Phase 3 ditches plausibly combined drainage with social functions such as plot marking, while wetland use coexisted with nearby dryland cultivation; the sources cannot separate hydrological, tenure and risk-management drivers.

sources.supports: Wetland/dryland comparison and explicitly alternative social/ecological explanations.

counterevidence: Archaeology records channels more readily than rules, rights, intentions or dryland maintenance.
inference_limits: Contemporary ethnographic analogies do not establish ancient owners, coercion or division of labor.

test.mechanism_chain: Water and/or competing plot claims -> channel digging and maintenance -> drainable and demarcated cultivation spaces
test.strongest_rival: Primarily hydrological adaptation versus primarily territorial demarcation; both predict channels
test.discriminating_observation: Ditch layout versus hydraulic gradient and field boundaries, repair histories, independent tenure/settlement evidence
test.evidence_sought_found: S10 reports hierarchical and nonhierarchical networks and reviews several motivations
test.remaining_ambiguity: Ancient property institutions and labor control remain unknown; functional coexistence does not distinguish primary cause

statement: The Phase 3–4 sequence at Kuk contains a several-hundred-year gap in wetland cultivation, while the reason remains unresolved among hydrological change, dryland alternatives and social disruption; it does not demonstrate disappearance of cultivation knowledge.

sources.supports: Later Phase 3 around 2700–2500 years ago, Phase 4 around 2000 years ago; competing abandonment explanations.

counterevidence: Occupation or gardening beyond the sampled wetland could continue; other valleys have insufficient resolution for simultaneous cessation.
inference_limits: Local discontinuity is not a culture-wide technological loss or regional failure.

test.mechanism_chain: Changed water, alternatives or social access -> wetland maintenance ends -> detectable gap before later ditch configuration
test.strongest_rival: Loss of know-how versus deliberate reallocation or exclusion from workable land
test.discriminating_observation: Synchronous local water rise, changes in dryland crops/settlement, or evidence of population displacement preceding cessation
test.evidence_sought_found: S10 explicitly identifies the alternatives and says the precise reason is unknown
test.remaining_ambiguity: Available chronology does not select a cause; knowledge persistence leaves limited material traces

statement: At M24/11 in northern Te Waipounamu, the 2024 study associates probable kūmara starch and other proposed crop remains with fourteenth-century cultivation contexts and identifies later kūmara remains after 1650.

sources.supports: Context-specific microbotany, short-life dates and later deposits.

counterevidence: Taxonomic identification relies on morphology and context; crop-abundance inference is not directly proportional to surviving starch counts.
inference_limits: No continent-wide arrival date, harvest quantity, uninterrupted cultivation or universal disappearance of other crops.

test.reason: Reports bounded site evidence and authors’ probabilistic taxonomic interpretations.

statement: The Cook Strait experimental gardens demonstrate feasible growth of selected Māori kūmara cultivars under 1999–2002 conditions, but modern plant treatment, fencing, windbreaks, unreplicated plots and nontraditional storage prevent treating their yields as ancient farm performance.

sources.supports: Trial design, returned/tissue-cultured collection, results, storage caveat and limits.

counterevidence: The experiments were explicitly exploratory and iwi authorities were consulted; these limits do not make practical growth results worthless.
inference_limits: Per-hectare extrapolation from tiny plots is not measured ancient output, adoption or labor productivity.

test.reason: Separates an observed feasibility demonstration from historical adoption and causal comparison.

statement: At Pōhatu, the 2025 collaborative study used Mana Whenua knowledge to guide questions and interpret modified soils; weak support for initially considered marine fertilizers led to further testing of terrestrial plant inputs, with kānuka a plausible rather than certain source.

sources.supports: Research sequence, knowledge-guided interpretation, gravel additions and fertilizer alternatives.

counterevidence: Geochemical signatures are not unique; only two profiles and selected candidate amendments were examined.
inference_limits: Knowledge systems contribute different evidence and meanings; agreement is not blanket authentication of all historical details.

test.mechanism_chain: Place-linked knowledge and shared questions -> targeted soil sampling and interpretation -> candidate amendments revised through joint discussion -> bounded reconstruction
test.strongest_rival: Soil chemistry alone would yield the same conclusions, or any favored tradition could be fitted after the fact
test.discriminating_observation: Documented sequence in which an initial candidate fails, further candidates are proposed, and tests discriminate rather than merely affirm
test.evidence_sought_found: S12 section4.3 describes marine hypotheses failing Mn matching and expanded plant testing; sections1–3 document prior collaboration
test.remaining_ambiguity: No parallel research team without community input; exact ancient fertilizer and timing remain uncertain

statement: Pōhatu’s contemporary investigation is framed by Mana Whenua as recovery of place-based cultivation knowledge after land alienation and disconnection; the published study supports reconnection and food-sovereignty aspirations but does not measure restored horticultural adoption.

sources.supports: Private ownership over 150 years, displacement narrative, research questions and intended restoration.

counterevidence: Historical land-transfer details rely partly on cited scholarship and community history, not a deed audit in this contribution.
inference_limits: Do not convert an aspiration or research partnership into a completed livelihood transition.

test.reason: Distinguishes documented research purpose and historical account from unmeasured deployment outcomes.

statement: The Martu study describes customary rights to burn, possible retribution for burning others’ areas, and social value attached to care for Country; localized burning was not institution-free individual optimization.

sources.locator: Materials and Methods, paragraphs on social/economic disincentives and kanyinin/Jukurrpa
sources.supports: Ethnographic account of rights, costs, responsibilities and public-good recognition.

counterevidence: Norms and sanctions are described by researchers, not quantified as an independent enforcement dataset.
inference_limits: No claim that all Martu follow identical rules, that enforcement is equal, or that social incentives alone determine fire outcomes.

test.reason: Records the published ethnographic account of governance and meanings without assigning isolated causal weights.

statement: Enomoto reports 436 hunting firearms among 955 Shiiba-mountain households in 1745 and 586 firearms in 1836; these are local recorded stocks, not a national ownership rate.

sources.supports: Counts inherited from Fujiki, Katanagari, pp. 168–169.

counterevidence: Household denominator for 1836 is not supplied; recorded ownership may exclude unlicensed guns.
inference_limits: Original village registers not inspected; neither persons armed nor annual use can be calculated.

test.reason: Bounded description of a published local example.

statement: Legal crop-protection and hunting use, together with recorded commoner ownership, contradicts a general account of Tokugawa Japan eliminating guns.

sources.supports: Local firearm records and distinctions among possession, carriage and use.
Common rural firearms and farm-tool uses.
Continued elite and non-elite peacetime niches.

counterevidence: Restrictions and confiscations occurred; persistence does not imply unchanged military effectiveness or unconstrained ownership.
inference_limits: Sources share Japanese historical scholarship; high confidence applies to rejecting total elimination, not to national abundance.

test.reason: Tests a categorical absence claim using positive local evidence; no causal estimate of regulation.

statement: Task-specific permission and peacetime elite appropriation helped accommodate continued firearm use within Tokugawa hierarchies, rather than requiring universal rejection of the technology.

sources.supports: Differentiated regulation and village use.
Licensed commoner use and elite marksmanship/status.

counterevidence: Enforcement weakness or unofficial circulation could also sustain guns; no estimate of their relative weight.
inference_limits: This is a scoped accommodation mechanism, not proof that peace or hierarchy caused a national innovation slowdown.

test.mechanism_chain: Crop/hunting needs and elite interests -> authorities authorize differentiated uses -> firearms retain legitimate niches -> persistence under regulation.
test.strongest_rival: Persistence merely reflects inability to enforce a universal ban.
test.discriminating_observation: Officially acknowledged permissible uses and elite use, not only illicit caches.
test.evidence_sought_found: S01 records authorized local possession; S03 summarizes regulated farming and elite marksmanship.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No matched-domain enforcement comparison; peace, status and livelihood incentives co-evolve.

statement: Howell interprets a shift in Edo-hinterland gun meanings from farm implements toward weapons in the 1840s as responding to anxiety about rural disorder.

sources.supports: Author states the 1840s change and disorder interpretation.

counterevidence: The study might also reflect changing enforcement, reporting vocabulary or later military developments.
inference_limits: Abstract-only access; no independently inspected beliefs, petitions or individual trajectory.

test.mechanism_chain: Perceived disorder -> villagers reinterpret guns as defensive weapons -> social use/meaning changes.
test.strongest_rival: A change in record language or administrative classification rather than in actual behavior.
test.discriminating_observation: Contemporaneous petitions and firing/use records showing changes before external military rearmament.
test.evidence_sought_found: S02 abstract gives the interpretation; underlying examples were unavailable.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cannot separate behavior, rhetoric and selection from the abstract.

statement: Guan, Palma and Wu distinguish full silver convertibility (1260–76), nominal convertibility (1277–1309) and a fiat regime from 1310; exchange availability and official status were distinct.

sources.supports: Authors reconstruct regime stages and spatially unequal redemption access.

counterevidence: Exact transition boundaries vary by one year in parts of manuscript; local availability could diverge from legal promise.
inference_limits: Periodization is historians’ reconstruction; no uniform household access is inferred.

test.reason: Description of reconstructed monetary configurations.

statement: The study’s reconstructed respectability CPI estimates annual inflation of 11.0% for 1260–1290, 1.8% for 1290–1340 and 4.5% for 1340–1355, contradicting uniform century-long hyperinflation.

sources.supports: Price basket, sparse observations, interpolation, and reported compound rates.

counterevidence: Individual prices and regions differed; the final collapse extends beyond 1355 price data.
inference_limits: About a dozen observations per commodity with interpolation/extrapolation; modelled index, not modern continuous official CPI. No household cost-of-living equivalence.

test.reason: Reports the authors’ bounded calculation and its measurement method.

statement: In the reconstructed 1260–1355 series, civil-war frequency correlates with greater nominal and real note issuance; imperial grants do not show comparable statistical associations in Table 4.

sources.supports: Civil-war coefficients and distinctions among nominal/real issues and rival demands.

counterevidence: Natural disasters weakly correlate with real issuance at the 10% level; external-war coefficients are not significant.
inference_limits: Political disorder, inflation and fiscal erosion can reinforce each other. No exogenous shock identifies the fiscal channel; absence of significance is not proof of no effect.

test.mechanism_chain: Civil conflict -> fiscal demands/tax difficulty -> greater note issuance -> potential pressure on currency value.
test.strongest_rival: Inflation and collapsing revenue cause civil conflict; or imperial grants/disasters dominate spending.
test.discriminating_observation: Different associations for war types and grants, with temporally ordered independently measured fiscal shortages.
test.evidence_sought_found: S04 Table 4 finds civil-war associations in nominal/real issues, no grant association, and weak real-disaster associations; only sparse fiscal totals.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Annual reconstructed time series does not remove reciprocal causation or omitted political changes; fiscal intermediate evidence incomplete.

statement: Yuan legal monetary unification coexisted with regional and task-specific practices: Ichimaru reports different uses of guanwen and dingliang, while Guan et al. report silver property transactions despite official restrictions.

sources.supports: Regional account-unit and government/commercial distinctions.
Private silver use and Yunnan cowry exception.

counterevidence: A regional unit of account is not automatically a different circulating medium.
inference_limits: Contract-level evidence in S05 not inspected; formal legal-tender scope must not be equated with every transaction.

statement: Polo’s paper-money narrative combines threat of punishment for refusal with portability, official authentication and damaged-note replacement; it cannot independently establish willing universal acceptance.
